Bed pressures lead to rushed transfers where the checklist is skipped → audit out-of-hours and high-occupancy periods specifically.
Discrepancies found are not escalated → add a clear 'what to do if a discrepancy is found' step to the checklist.
pearls: Use the same transfer checklist already required for other information (e.g. VTE status, allergies) so this is one extra line, not a new form.
Train bed managers and site teams on the importance of this final identity check.
Report any discrepancies found as safety learning, in addition to the completion rate.
Re-audit at a different time of year to check winter bed-pressure periods are not worse.
effort: ~15 min per 10 transfers from checklists
pass: The transfer checklist or handover documentation records that the identity band was checked against the patient and/or case notes at the point of transfer

question: What proportion of adult inpatients who have bed rails fitted have an individual written risk assessment completed before the bed rails are used?
why: Bed rails carry a risk of fatal chest or neck entrapment, listed as a Never Event; an individual risk assessment before use is the main safeguard, and no audit of this step has been published in the library.

standard.source: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023)
standard.wording: Chest or neck entrapment in bed rails is listed (number 11) as a 'Never Event' according to the NHS in 2018... Risk assessments should account for any characteristics which might put the bed user at greater risk from use of bed rails.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients with bed rails in use on a general ward. Exclusion: cot-side rails on paediatric beds.
sample: 40 inpatients with bed rails in use, identified across 4 wards on the same day
data_source: Moving and handling / bed rail risk assessment documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the bed rail risk assessment a mandatory EPR step that must be completed before a 'bed rails in use' order can be entered, using a standard entrapment-risk checklist.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same spot-check method and sample size
close_loop: Present at the patient safety committee (Never Events); embed the mandatory EPR step trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of individual bed rail risk assessment completion found in the library]
pitfalls: Bed rails put up as a default without individual assessment → make the assessment a prerequisite in the EPR order.
Risk assessment done once on admission and not reviewed when the patient's condition changes → audit whether it is reviewed after any relevant change.
Staff underestimate entrapment risk because they see bed rails as routine → include Never Event learning in ward teaching.
Assessment completed but not accessible to night staff → keep it in a single, easy-to-find EPR location.
pearls: Use the MHRA's example adult entrapment risk assessment checklist as the basis for the EPR form.
Involve the moving and handling/tissue viability team in reviewing findings.
Report any Never Event near-misses found during the audit immediately through the incident system.
Repeat the spot-check on wards with higher rates of confusion or frailty.
effort: ~20 min per ward round of 10 patients
pass: A documented, individualised bed rail risk assessment (considering the patient's size, mobility, confusion or agitation, and bed/mattress configuration) is completed and filed before the bed rails are fitted

question: What proportion of decisions to use bed rails are documented with the reasoning, and evidence that this was explained to the patient or their family?
why: Because bed rails restrict a patient's movement and carry entrapment risk, the decision to use them should be individually justified and, where possible, discussed with the patient; no audit of documented reasoning and communication has been published in the library.

standard.source: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023)
standard.wording: Every effort should be made to explain to the person being cared for why their bed has or is likely to have bed rails fitted. The potential risks, as identified by their individual risk assessment should also be explained to the person, as appropriate... The decision to use bed rails should be made with the person's consent, wherever possible.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients with bed rails in use. Exclusion: none.
sample: 40 inpatients with bed rails in use, identified across 4 wards on the same day
data_source: Bed rail risk assessment and nursing notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add 'reason explained to patient/family' and 'consent/best interests' as mandatory fields on the bed rail risk assessment form, alongside the risk assessment itself.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same spot-check method and sample size
close_loop: Present at the patient safety committee; embed the mandatory fields trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of documented reasoning and consent for bed rail use found in the library]
pitfalls: Explanation given verbally but not recorded → add a specific field rather than relying on general nursing notes.
Patients who lack capacity are not covered by a best-interests decision → link the field to the trust's Mental Capacity Act documentation.
Family not contactable at the time bed rails are first used → record this and require follow-up documentation once contact is made.
Staff see this as extra paperwork → combine it with the risk assessment form so it is one document, not two.
pearls: Combine this audit with the risk-assessment-before-use audit as one bed rails safety audit.
Provide a simple patient/family information leaflet on bed rails to support the conversation.
Involve the mental capacity/best interests lead where patients lack capacity.
Share good-practice examples of clear documentation at ward teaching sessions.
effort: ~15 min per ward round of 10 patients
pass: The notes record the reason bed rails were prescribed, that this was explained to the patient (or their family/representative if the patient lacks capacity), and whether consent was given

question: What proportion of beds with bed rails fitted are checked each shift for gaps or configuration changes that could increase the risk of entrapment?
why: Entrapment risk changes if the mattress, bed or rail configuration changes, or is replaced, after the original risk assessment; no audit of ongoing shift-by-shift bed rail safety checks has been published in the library.

standard.source: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023)
standard.wording: What configuration of bed, mattress and rail system is being used?... Our adverse incident investigations have shown that the physical or clinical condition of bed occupants means that some are at greater risk of entrapment in bed rails.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients with bed rails in use on a general ward. Exclusion: none.
sample: 30 patients with bed rails, checked over 3 consecutive shifts each, over 2-4 weeks
data_source: Direct observation and shift handover/intentional rounding documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a bed rail configuration check to the twice-daily intentional rounding checklist, prompting a repeat risk assessment whenever the bed, mattress or rail is changed.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same method and sample size
close_loop: Present at the patient safety committee (Never Events); embed the check into intentional rounding trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of shift-by-shift bed rail configuration checks found in the library]
pitfalls: Mattress replaced (e.g. for pressure relief) without repeating the bed rail check → link mattress ordering to an automatic bed rail re-check prompt.
Checks become a tick-box exercise without real inspection → include a photo-based training aid on what to look for.
Night shift checks are less thorough → include night shifts explicitly in the sample.
Staff unfamiliar with entrapment zones → provide the MHRA entrapment-area diagram at the nursing station.
pearls: Combine with other intentional rounding items (pressure area care, hydration) so it is one round.
Use the MHRA entrapment risk-area diagram for staff training.
Involve estates/equipment teams when a mismatched bed and mattress combination is found.
Report any hazards found immediately, not only in the aggregate audit result.
effort: ~15 min per shift check of 10 patients
pass: A documented shift check confirms the bed, mattress and rail configuration matches what was risk-assessed, with no new gaps, and flags any change for a repeat risk assessment

question: What proportion of safeguarding concerns identified for adult inpatients with care and support needs have a safeguarding referral made and documented on the day the concern is identified?
why: A prompt safeguarding referral allows the local authority to assess and act quickly to protect an adult at risk; no audit of the timeliness of making the referral itself (as opposed to the outcome of the safeguarding process) has been published in the library.

standard.source: Department of Health and Social Care, Care and support statutory guidance (Care Act 2014), paragraph 14.7
standard.wording: Safeguarding means protecting an adult's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. It is about people and organisations working together to prevent and stop both the risks and experience of abuse or neglect.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients for whom a safeguarding concern (suspected abuse, neglect or self-neglect) is identified and documented by ward staff in the last 3-6 months. Exclusion: concerns identified and referred before admission by another agency.
sample: 30 consecutive safeguarding concerns identified on adult wards over the last 3-6 months
data_source: Safeguarding referral log, ward safeguarding documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a same-day safeguarding referral task to the EPR whenever a safeguarding concern is documented, with an automatic reminder to the named nurse or ward manager if the referral has not been submitted by the end of the shift.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the trust safeguarding adults committee; embed the automatic EPR task trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of same-day safeguarding referral timeliness for adult inpatients found in the library]
pitfalls: Staff are unsure whether a concern meets the referral threshold and delay while seeking advice → provide a same-day advice line staffed by the trust safeguarding team.
Concerns identified out of hours wait until the next working day → confirm an out-of-hours referral route exists and is used.
Small numbers of qualifying concerns on general wards → extend sampling to 6 months or pool several wards.
Referral made verbally to a colleague but not formally submitted → audit only formal referrals recorded in the safeguarding log.
pearls: Work with the trust safeguarding adults lead to define what counts as 'identified' versus 'referred'.
Provide a laminated safeguarding referral pathway card on every ward.
Report both the same-day rate and the reasons for any delay found.
Re-audit after staff safeguarding training to see if the change has had an effect.
effort: ~20 min per 10 concerns from the safeguarding log
pass: A safeguarding concern/referral form is completed and submitted to the local authority safeguarding team on the same calendar day the concern is identified and documented by staff

question: What proportion of adult inpatients who receive rapid tranquillisation have their pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness monitored at least hourly afterwards?
why: Rapid tranquillisation carries a risk of cardiorespiratory depression, and physical monitoring is the safeguard against this; no audit of post-rapid-tranquillisation physical monitoring on general hospital wards (as opposed to mental health units) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.4.45 (2015)
standard.wording: After rapid tranquillisation, monitor side effects and the service user's pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, level of hydration and level of consciousness at least every hour until there are no further concerns about their physical health status. Monitor every 15 minutes if the BNF maximum dose has been exceeded or the service user...

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients on a general medical or surgical ward who receive parenteral rapid tranquillisation for acute behavioural disturbance. Exclusion: patients on a mental health ward already covered by a dedicated rapid tranquillisation monitoring protocol.
sample: 30 consecutive episodes of rapid tranquillisation on general wards over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Observation chart, drug administration record, incident report
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a dedicated post-rapid-tranquillisation monitoring chart (paper or electronic) that pre-populates the six required parameters and the hourly (or 15-minute) schedule automatically when the drug is recorded as given.
reaudit: 6-12 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety committee and violence-reduction/security steering group; embed the dedicated chart trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of post-rapid-tranquillisation physical monitoring on general wards found in the library]
pitfalls: Rapid tranquillisation episodes are uncommon on general wards, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period to 6-12 months across the whole trust.
Standard NEWS2 charts do not capture hydration or consciousness in the way needed → use a dedicated chart rather than the routine observation chart.
Staff are focused on managing the acute behavioural disturbance and monitoring is deprioritised → assign a named member of staff to monitoring at the time the drug is given.
Episodes are not all captured on the incident system → cross-check against pharmacy records of parenteral sedatives given.
pearls: Involve the mental health liaison team, who are often called to these episodes on general wards.
Use a pre-printed sticker or EPR order set that starts the monitoring schedule automatically.
Review every episode with a debrief involving the nurse in charge, not only the aggregate percentage.
Track any adverse events (oversedation, respiratory depression) alongside the audit as an outcome measure.
effort: ~20 min per episode from observation charts and drug records
pass: All six parameters (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration status, level of consciousness) are documented at least hourly for the period following rapid tranquillisation until concerns have resolved

question: What proportion of documented episodes of manual restraint on adult wards record that the least restrictive intervention was used and the reasons for the level of restriction chosen?
why: Using and recording the least restrictive intervention protects patients' rights and reduces harm; no audit of whether this specific documentation standard is met (as opposed to whether a post-incident debrief is offered) has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.1.9 (2015)
standard.wording: Ensure that service users understand that during any restrictive intervention their human rights will be respected and the least restrictive intervention will be used to enable them to exercise their rights... Identify and reduce any barriers to a service user exercising their rights and, if this is not possible, record the reasons in their notes.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients physically restrained on a general medical, surgical or mental health ward in the last 6-12 months. Exclusion: brief supportive holds during a medical procedure with the patient's cooperation.
sample: 30 consecutive restraint episodes over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Restraint/restrictive intervention incident form
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add mandatory fields to the restraint incident form for 'less restrictive options considered' and 'reason for level of restriction used', which must be completed before the form can be closed.
reaudit: 6-12 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the restrictive practice reduction group; embed the mandatory fields trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [NNA-147] patients offered a documented chance to talk about a restraint incident within 72 hours (a related but distinct documentation requirement in the same NG10 guideline)
pitfalls: Incident forms focus on what happened rather than why that level of restriction was chosen → add specific fields rather than free text alone.
Staff under time pressure after an incident complete the form minimally → allow the form to be completed in two stages (immediate facts, then reflection within 24 hours).
Small numbers of restraint episodes on general wards → extend the sampling period.
Different staff have different thresholds for what counts as 'least restrictive' → provide training and examples.
pearls: Run this alongside the existing post-incident debrief audit so the whole NG10 documentation standard is reviewed together.
Involve service user representatives in reviewing what good documentation looks like.
Use restrictive intervention reduction programme data (already required by NG10) as a source of episodes.
Share themes from the reasons documented, not just the completion rate, to guide training.
effort: ~20 min per episode from incident forms
pass: The restraint incident record documents that a less restrictive option was considered, and states the reason the level of restriction used was chosen

question: What proportion of adult inpatients have an oral health/mouth care assessment completed within 24 hours of admission?
why: An early mouth care assessment identifies patients who need help maintaining oral hygiene, reducing the risk of infection, discomfort and reduced nutritional intake; no audit of mouth care assessment completion has been published in the library.

standard.source: Health Education England, Mouth Care Matters (2019), cited in a hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157
standard.wording: It is suggested by (NHS Health Education Mouth Care Matters 2019) a mouth care assessment should be undertaken on admission or within 24 hours of admission and should be reviewed weekly.

population: Inclusion: adults admitted to a general medical or surgical ward for 24 hours or more. Exclusion: day-case admissions.
sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions over the last 4 weeks
data_source: EPR nursing admission assessment / mouth care assessment tool
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory mouth care assessment field to the electronic nursing admission assessment for every adult inpatient.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the tissue viability/nutrition and hydration steering group; embed the mandatory field trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no closed-loop audit of mouth care assessment completion found in the library]
pitfalls: Mouth care assessment seen as a low priority compared with other admission tasks → make it part of the same mandatory admission bundle as pressure ulcer and falls risk assessment.
Staff lack confidence assessing the mouth without dental training → provide short Mouth Care Matters training and a simple visual guide.
Assessment done but not reviewed weekly as required → track weekly review as a separate, later measure.
Patients with dentures or dysphagia need a modified approach not captured by a simple tool → add a free-text note field for these cases.
pearls: Use the trust's existing Mouth Care Matters-based assessment tool rather than creating a new one.
Provide a basic mouth care kit at every bedside so assessment leads straight into action.
Involve speech and language therapy for patients with dysphagia identified through the assessment.
Report results alongside pressure ulcer and falls assessment rates, since all three are part of the same admission bundle.
effort: ~15 min per 10 admissions from EPR
pass: A mouth care assessment screening tool is completed and documented within 24 hours of admission

question: What proportion of adult inpatients assessed as needing help with mouth care (amber or red on the mouth care assessment) receive documented mouth care at least twice daily?
why: Patients who cannot manage their own oral hygiene depend on nursing staff to deliver mouth care reliably; no audit of the frequency of delivered mouth care for dependent patients has been published in the library.

standard.source: Hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157, applying Health Education England's Mouth Care Matters standard
standard.wording: Independent (Green), promote good oral mouth health care as a minimum of twice daily; Needs supervision/help to clean teeth (Amber)... Needs mouth care (Red), assist with mouth care.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients scored amber or red on the mouth care assessment, in hospital for 3 or more days. Exclusion: patients discharged within 48 hours of assessment.
sample: 30 consecutive amber/red patients, reviewed over 3 days each, over the last 4-8 weeks
data_source: EPR daily care round / mouth care recording sheet
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add mouth care to the twice-daily intentional rounding checklist for every patient scored amber or red, with a signature box for each round.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the tissue viability/nutrition and hydration steering group; embed the intentional rounding item trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no closed-loop audit of mouth care delivery frequency for dependent patients found in the library]
pitfalls: Mouth care given but not recorded → build recording into the same electronic round as repositioning and hydration.
Staff shortages mean mouth care is deprioritised against other tasks → make it an explicit, named item on the intentional rounding chart rather than assumed.
Patients who are nil by mouth are wrongly assumed not to need mouth care → clarify that NBM patients need mouth care even more, not less.
Reduced consciousness or intubated patients need a different technique not distinguished on a simple chart → add a note field for special techniques used.
pearls: Stock basic mouth care kits (sponge sticks, non-foaming toothpaste) on every bed bay.
Train healthcare assistants specifically, since they often deliver most mouth care.
Combine this audit with the mouth care assessment audit to review the full pathway.
Report results by ward, since dependency levels vary a great deal between specialties.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR care round records
pass: For a patient scored amber or red on the mouth care assessment, documented mouth care is recorded at least twice in each 24-hour period

question: What proportion of omitted or delayed doses of a medicine flagged as time-critical are documented with a reason on the drug chart or eMAR?
why: Recording why a time-critical dose was omitted or delayed lets pharmacy and nursing teams identify and fix recurring causes; no audit of the completeness of omission-reason coding for time-critical medicines specifically has been published in the library.

standard.source: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Defining time critical medicines (reviewed 2024/2025)
standard.wording: Those where early or delayed administration of maintenance doses of greater than 30 minutes before or after the scheduled dose may cause harm or result in substantial sub-optimal therapy.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients prescribed a medicine on the ward's local time-critical medicines list (e.g. levodopa, short-acting insulin, anti-epileptics, immunosuppressants). Exclusion: medicines stopped altogether by a prescriber (not an omission).
sample: 40 consecutive omitted or delayed time-critical doses identified from the eMAR over the last 4-8 weeks
data_source: Electronic medicines administration record omission/delay report
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make the omission/delay reason a mandatory coded field in the eMAR (rather than optional free text) whenever a time-critical medicine is recorded as omitted or given late.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the medicines safety committee; embed the mandatory coded field trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [ONA-121] and [NNA-095] audit whether Parkinson's time-critical doses are given on time; no audit of the completeness of reason-coding for missed or delayed time-critical doses found in the library
pitfalls: Reason entered as vague free text ('N/A') that does not explain the cause → use a fixed drop-down list of reason categories.
Staff do not know which medicines on the chart are time-critical → flag them visually on the eMAR.
Doses omitted overnight are under-documented due to lower staffing → include night shifts in the sample.
Reason coding varies between wards using paper versus electronic charts → restrict the audit to wards on the same eMAR system for consistency.
pearls: Agree the trust's time-critical medicines list with pharmacy before starting data collection.
Use the coded reasons to run a monthly pharmacy-led review of recurring causes.
Pair this audit with the specific Parkinson's and insulin timing audits to build a full picture.
Feed back common reasons (e.g. 'medicine not available') to procurement or ward stock processes.
effort: ~20 min per 10 omitted/delayed doses from the eMAR
pass: Every omitted or more-than-30-minutes-delayed dose of a medicine on the ward's time-critical medicines list has a coded or documented reason entered on the eMAR

question: What proportion of elective surgical patients who are cancelled or delayed on the day of surgery are offered food or drink within 1 hour of being told they will not have surgery that day?
why: Patients who have fasted appropriately for a planned procedure that is then cancelled or significantly delayed are at risk of unnecessary prolonged starvation and dehydration if this is not acted on promptly; no audit of this specific step for elective (non-trauma) lists has been published in the library.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland recommended fasting times, cited in the PIER Network Peri-operative Fasting Policy (October 2020)
standard.wording: Excessive fasting can cause a great deal of stress for children and their carers... Excessive fasting leads to irritability and agitation whilst waiting for surgery.

population: Inclusion: adult elective surgical inpatients cancelled or delayed by more than 2 hours past their scheduled time in the last 4-8 weeks. Exclusion: cancellations where the patient needs to remain fasted for a same-day rescheduled procedure.
sample: 30 consecutive cancelled or significantly delayed elective patients over the last 4-8 weeks
data_source: Ward nursing notes, theatre cancellation log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'cancelled: may eat and drink now?' step to the theatre coordinator's cancellation process, with a scripted phone call to the ward and a timed nursing task to offer food and drink.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the theatres governance meeting; embed the cancellation step trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [ONA-147] similar standard already used for trauma list cancellations (a related audit limited to trauma lists); no closed-loop audit for elective general surgical list cancellations found in the library
pitfalls: Communication delay between theatres and the ward means the ward is unaware of the cancellation → use a direct phone call, not just an electronic list update.
Patient still due to be rescheduled later the same day so remains fasted appropriately → record this as a valid reason, not a failure.
Cancellations late in the day are under-recorded because staff focus on other tasks → include all times of day in the sample.
No consistent record of when the patient was actually told → agree a single point of documentation (nursing notes) for this time.
pearls: Give the theatre coordinator a one-line script to use when phoning the ward.
Track patient-reported experience of cancellation alongside the audit as a balancing measure.
Share cancellation and fasting-related complaints with the theatres team to reinforce the case for change.
Re-audit during a busy winter period to test the process under pressure.
effort: ~15 min per 10 cases from theatre and ward records
pass: A documented offer of food or drink (or a stated clinical reason why this is not yet possible) is recorded within 1 hour of the patient being informed their operation will not go ahead that day

question: What proportion of restrictive intervention decisions for patients who lack capacity involve documented consultation with a carer or family member, in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
why: Involving carers and family in decisions about restrictive interventions for patients who lack capacity is both a legal requirement and a safeguard against unnecessary restriction; no audit of this specific documentation standard has been published in the library.

standard.source: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.1.10 (2015)
standard.wording: Ensure that carers are involved in decision-making whenever possible, if the service user agrees, and that carers are involved in decision-making for all service users who lack mental capacity, in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients who lack capacity (as documented under the Mental Capacity Act) and are subject to a restrictive intervention decision. Exclusion: patients who have capacity and consent to the intervention themselves.
sample: 30 consecutive qualifying restrictive intervention episodes over the last 6-12 months
data_source: Restraint/restrictive intervention incident form, Mental Capacity Act assessment documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'carer/family consulted (or reason why not)' field to the restrictive intervention incident form, linked to the Mental Capacity Act assessment section.
reaudit: 6-12 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the restrictive practice reduction group and Mental Capacity Act steering group; embed the mandatory field trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of carer/family consultation documentation for restrictive interventions in patients lacking capacity found in the library]
pitfalls: Urgent situations mean consultation happens after, not before, the intervention → accept and record retrospective consultation as long as it is documented promptly.
No carer or family member is contactable → record this explicitly rather than leaving the field blank.
Capacity assessment itself is not documented, making the population hard to define → run this audit alongside a capacity-documentation check.
Staff conflate 'informing' a family member after the event with 'involving' them in the decision → clarify the distinction in training.
pearls: Link this audit to the trust's existing Mental Capacity Act training programme.
Involve the safeguarding and mental capacity leads in reviewing findings.
Provide a quick-reference card on when and how to contact carers out of hours.
Report findings alongside the least-restrictive-intervention audit for a fuller picture of NG10 compliance.
effort: ~20 min per episode from incident forms
pass: For a patient who lacks capacity at the time of a restrictive intervention decision, the notes document that a carer or family member was consulted, or record why this was not possible

question: What proportion of adult inpatients on a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion have their capillary blood glucose measured at least hourly?
why: Hourly glucose monitoring during a variable-rate insulin infusion is essential to detect and prevent both hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia promptly; no audit of monitoring frequency during a running infusion (as opposed to the response once a hypo has already occurred) has been published in the library.

standard.source: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, JBDS 01: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023)
standard.wording: If the person was on IV insulin, continue to check blood glucose every 15 minutes until...

population: Inclusion: adult inpatients on a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion on a general ward. Exclusion: patients in critical care with continuous glucose monitoring already in place.
sample: 30 consecutive patients on a variable-rate insulin infusion, reviewed over their first 12 hours on the infusion, over the last 3 months
data_source: EPR glucose monitoring record, insulin infusion prescription chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the EPR insulin infusion order to automatically schedule and prompt hourly glucose-check tasks for the duration of the infusion.
reaudit: 6 months after the change, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the diabetes inpatient steering group; embed the automatic scheduling trust-wide if the target is met.
evidence: [NNA-116] repeat glucose check within 15 minutes after a hypo on treatment (a related but distinct audit of the response to a low reading, not routine hourly monitoring)
pitfalls: Glucose checks recorded on a separate paper chart not linked to the EPR infusion order → move monitoring into the same electronic system as the infusion.
Checks clustered together after a gap rather than genuinely hourly → measure the longest gap, not just the total number of checks.
Ward staffing pressure causes delays overnight → include night hours specifically in the sample.
Infusion stopped and restarted multiple times, complicating the 12-hour window → record only the first continuous run.
pearls: Use networked glucose meters that time-stamp readings automatically to reduce data collection effort.
Involve the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse team in reviewing outlying cases.
Track hypoglycaemia and severe hyperglycaemia rates on infusions as an outcome measure alongside monitoring frequency.
Re-audit on wards less familiar with insulin infusions, such as surgical wards, separately from specialist diabetes wards.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR glucose records
pass: Local standard, applying the JBDS principle of frequent glucose monitoring during IV insulin therapy: capillary blood glucose is documented at least once every hour while the variable-rate insulin infusion is running
